_comment: Introductions shown beneath the hero on each book page. Keyed by page slug rather than book name: book_blurbs.json derives its key by slugifying the name it carries, which silently lost Al-Tawḥīd and Muʿjam al-Aḥādīth al-Muʿtabara when that name did not match the catalogue's.
al-kafi: Compiled by Muḥammad b. Yaʿqūb al-Kulaynī (d. 329/941) over roughly twenty years, al-Kāfi is the earliest of the Four Books and the most widely cited collection in Twelver Shi'ism. It is built in three parts. The Uṣūl gathers narrations on belief — the nature of reason, the oneness of God, prophethood, and the imamate. The Furūʿ covers practice and law across purity, prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, marriage, inheritance, trade and judgement. The Rawḍa, standing apart from both, collects sermons, letters and reports that fit no other heading. Its size is what makes it distinctive: where later compilers selected, al-Kulaynī recorded, and much of what survives of the earlier written sources of the tradition survives because it passed through here.
man-la-yahduruh-al-faqih: The second of the Four Books, written by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) for a patron in Balkh who had no scholar nearby to consult. Its title — 'for one who has no jurist at hand' — states its method: rather than record everything transmitted, al-Ṣadūq included only what he was prepared to rely on, saying he offered these reports as proof between himself and God. That editorial stance makes it the most opinionated of the Four Books, and the most practical. Chains are usually shortened or omitted in the text itself, with the full paths set out separately in the mashyakha at the end, so the reader meets the ruling first and the transmission afterwards.
nahj-al-balagha: Sermons, letters and short sayings of Imam ʿAlī, selected by al-Sharīf al-Raḍī (d. 406/1015) — himself a poet — for their eloquence as much as their content. The arrangement follows that purpose: the sermons first, then the correspondence, then several hundred aphorisms. It ranges from the metaphysical to the immediately administrative, and includes the letter of instruction to Mālik al-Ashtar on governing Egypt, which is read as a treatise on just rule in its own right. Because al-Raḍī chose by literary criterion and often gave only the passage that moved him, the work has been studied as a monument of Arabic prose and as a doctrinal source, not always by the same readers.
al-amali: The 'dictations' of Shaykh al-Ṣadūq: not a compiled reference but a record of teaching sessions, each assembly dated and placed, delivered across Rayy, Nishapur and elsewhere. The material moves as a lesson moves — a narration on ethics, then one on the lives of the Prophet and the Imams, then a point of doctrine — rather than being sorted by subject. Read straight through, it shows what a leading scholar of the fourth century chose to put in front of an audience, and in what order, which is a different kind of evidence from a systematic collection.
al-khisal: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq's collection arranged entirely by number: traditions that enumerate one thing, then two, then three, ascending through the book. The ordering is a memory device rather than a subject index — it is how material was held before it was looked up — so a single chapter can move from the three things that ruin a person to the three that save him. The result is a book of enumerations spanning ethics, law, cosmology and history, and it preserves a good deal that appears nowhere else, including the long treatise on rights attributed to Imam Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn.
kitab-al-ghayba: Shaykh al-Ṭūsī (d. 460/1067) on the occultation of the twelfth Imam, written in Baghdad more than a century after the event it describes. It is not only a collection: al-Ṭūsī sets out the reports, then argues from them, then answers the objections of opponents directly — that a hidden leader is no leader, that the length of the concealment tells against it. It also documents the four deputies who are said to have carried communication during the shorter occultation, and the letters attributed to that period. It remains the principal early Imāmī treatment of the subject and the source most later discussions work from.
thawab-al-a-mal-wa-iqab-al-a-mal: Two complementary works of Shaykh al-Ṣadūq, usually printed and read as one: the rewards promised for particular acts, and the punishments warned of for particular sins. Each entry is short and specific — a prayer, a fast, a kindness, a betrayal — with the consequence attached. Taken together they map what the tradition treats as consequential rather than merely permitted or discouraged, and they are among the most quoted sources in sermons and popular devotional writing for exactly that reason.
uyun-akhbar-al-rida: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq's gathering of everything he could assemble concerning ʿAlī b. Mūsā al-Riḍā, the eighth Imam, composed for the Buyid vizier al-Ṣāḥib b. ʿAbbād. It runs from his sayings and correspondence to accounts of his journey to Khurāsān, his appointment as heir apparent by the caliph al-Maʾmūn, the debates he is recorded as holding at court with Christian, Jewish and Zoroastrian scholars, and the circumstances of his death. Because it is built around one figure rather than one subject, it reads as a life as much as a collection.
ma-ani-al-akhbar: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on the meanings of the reports: a collection assembled specifically to explain difficult words, obscure phrases and apparently strange statements found elsewhere in hadith. Its method is unusual — the explanation is itself a narration, so the book is a commentary built entirely out of other transmitted material rather than the compiler's own gloss. It is consulted when a report elsewhere is clear in its words and unclear in its sense.
kamil-al-ziyarat: Ibn Qūlawayh (d. 368/978), a teacher of al-Shaykh al-Mufīd, on ziyāra: the visitation of the Prophet and the Imams, and above all of Imam al-Ḥusayn at Karbalā — its merit, its rites, the words to be said, and the accounts of those who performed it. The book is cited nearly as often for its preface as its contents, because there the author states that he included only what reached him through reliable transmitters. Later scholars have disagreed sharply over whether that amounts to authenticating every chain in the book, and the question is still argued.
al-tawhid: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on divine unity, and the most sustained argument among his works. It gathers narrations on God's oneness, His names and attributes, His knowledge and will, and the rejection of any likeness between God and what He created. It was written against positions al-Ṣadūq regarded as errors on both sides — anthropomorphism on one, and a determinism that made human action meaningless on the other — and its arrangement follows that polemic, including several recorded debates in which the argument is carried out rather than asserted.
mu-jam-al-ahadith-al-mu-tabara: A modern compilation that admits only narrations meeting its compiler's stated criteria for reliability. The classical collections gather broadly and leave assessment to the reader; this one applies the assessment first, and says on what basis. That makes it useful for a particular question — which reports on a subject survive a strict standard — and it is best read alongside the older collections rather than instead of them, since what it excludes is as much a claim as what it keeps.
kitab-al-zuhd: An early collection by al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī, a companion of the eighth, ninth and tenth Imams, on renunciation: detachment from the world, restraint in appetite and speech, the remembrance of death, and the fear and hope the tradition treats as the proper posture toward God. Its author belongs to the generation whose written works the later compilers drew upon, so this is close to the raw material from which the large collections were built — short, unadorned, and organised by theme rather than argument.
kitab-al-du-afa: Not a hadith collection but a work of rijāl — the science of assessing transmitters. It consists of entries on narrators judged weak, unreliable, or worse, and it is consulted when weighing whether a chain of transmission can bear weight. Two things make it contested: its judgements are markedly more severe than those of comparable works, and its attribution to Aḥmad b. al-Ḥusayn Ibn al-Ghaḍāʾirī has itself been questioned, since the book reaches us through later citation rather than a continuous manuscript tradition. It is used, but rarely used alone.
kitab-al-mu-min: Al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī on the believer: the standing of a believer before God, and — the greater part of the book — the rights believers hold over one another. Visiting the sick, meeting a need, keeping a secret, withholding a harm: the narrations are concrete and the obligations mutual. Like its author's Kitāb al-Zuhd it is early, short and thematic, and it survives as one of the sources the later compilers had in front of them.
sifat-al-shi-a: A short collection by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on what the Shīʿa are held to be — the conduct, obligations and character the narrations attach to the name. It reads as a standard rather than a description: the reports describe how such a person prays, deals, speaks and bears difficulty, and several state plainly that the name without the conduct is not the thing. It is usually read together with Faḍaʾil al-Shīʿa, which takes the other side of the same subject.
risalat-al-huquq: The Treatise on Rights, attributed to Imam ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (d. 95/713), and unusual in this corpus for being one continuous argument rather than a gathering of separate reports. It enumerates around fifty rights in a single sustained sequence: the right of God, then of one's own tongue, hearing, sight and limbs, then of prayer and fasting, then of those one leads and follows, teaches and learns from, owns and owes, and finally of neighbours, companions and strangers. Each is stated as an obligation owed rather than a claim held, which is what gives the text its shape.
fada-il-al-shi-a: A brief collection by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on the merits promised to the Shīʿa — what is said to await those who hold to the Imams, in this life and after it. It is the companion piece to Ṣifāt al-Shīʿa: where that book sets out the conduct expected, this one sets out what is promised in return, and the two are ordinarily read and printed together.
